Furthermore, Euclidean distance searches over $\mathcal{F}$ can determine spectral resonances. Focusing on noise classification and identification rather than continuous power spectral density reconstruction makes $\mathcal{F}$ an efficient diagnostic tool for quantum hardware.
item.dc:creator: Chris Wise, Akram Youssry, Alberto Peruzzo, Jo Plested, Matt Woolley

item.title: Chirally frustrated superradiant phases in a Jaynes-Cummings trimer
item.description: arXiv:2507.13800v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the emergence of frustrated quantum phases in a Jaynes-Cummings (JC) trimer with complex hopping amplitudes between the cavities, which represents the smallest frustrated unit in light-matter systems. The complex hopping amplitudes that can be engineered via synthetic gauge fields introduce chiral effects and geometric frustration to the system. We obtain analytic solutions in the semiclassical limit and map out the phase diagram of this model, featuring one normal and three distinct superradiant phases. Among these phases, a chirally frustrated superradiant phase emerges, characterized by broken chiral and translational symmetries and unidirectional photon flow. These results reveal how frustration and symmetry breaking can arise in JC systems with synthetic gauge fields and strong light-matter coupling.
item.dc:creator: Lin-Lin Jiang, Ya-Ping Ni, Xuan Xie, Lin Tian, Jin-Feng Huang

item.title: Directional Codes for Quantum LDPC Error Correction on Square and Hexagonal Grid Architectures
item.description: arXiv:2507.19430v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Utility-scale quantum computing requires quantum error correction (QEC) to protect quantum information against noise. Currently, superconducting hardware is a promising candidate for achieving fault tolerance due to its fast gate times and feasible scalability. However, it is often restricted to two-dimensional nearest-neighbour connectivity, and therefore the variety of quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes that can be implemented on it without sacrificing QEC performance is believed to be greatly restricted. In this paper we construct a new family of qLDPC codes, which we call ``directional codes'', that outperforms the rotated toric code (RTC) while satisfying the connectivity requirements of the widely adopted square-grid, and some even the sparser hexagonal-grid, on a torus. The key idea is to utilise the iSWAP gate -- a native gate demonstrated on superconducting qubits -- to construct circuits that measure the stabilisers of these qLDPC codes without the need for additional connections. We numerically evaluate the performance of directional codes, encoding four, six, twelve and eighteen logical qubits, using a common superconducting-inspired circuit-level Pauli noise model. We also compare them to the RTC and to the bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, currently the two most popular quantum LDPC code families. As a concrete example, when evaluated with the Tesseract decoder with short beam setting, the best directional code family investigated achieves the same logical error rate as the RTC at physical error rate $p=10^{-3}$ but requires only a quarter to a third of the number of physical qubits to encode a given number of logical qubits. Our discovery opens a novel direction in QEC code design, suggesting that complex high-connectivity hardware may not be necessary for low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computation.
item.dc:creator: Gy\"orgy P. Geh\'er, David Byfield, Archibald Ruban

item.title: Symplectic Pauli-Schr\"odinger Equation for the Quark-Antiquark Interaction System
item.description: arXiv:2507.20045v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the quantum behavior of a quark-antiquark bound system under the influence of a magnetic field within the symplectic formulation of quantum mechanics. Employing a perturbative approach, we obtain the ground and first excited states of the system described by the Cornell potential, which incorporates both confining and non-confining interactions. After performing a Levi-Civita mapping in phase space, we solve the time-independent symplectic Pauli-Schr\"odinger-type equation and determine the corresponding Wigner function. Special attention is given to the observation of the confinement of the quark-antiquark, that is revealed in the phase space structure. Due to the presence of spin in the Hamiltonian, the results reveal that the magnetic field enhances the non-classicality of the Wigner function, signaling stronger quantum interference and a departure from classical behavior. The experimental mass spectra is used to estimate the intensity of the external field, leading to a value that is in order of the transiet magnetic field measured in non-central heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and LHC.
item.dc:creator: R. R. Luz, R. A. S. Paiva, G. X. A. Petronilo, A. E. Santana, T. M. Rocha Filho, R. G. G. Amorim

item.title: Hierarchy of entanglement detection criteria for random high-dimensional states
item.description: arXiv:2507.21787v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Entanglement is a cornerstone in quantum information science, yet detecting it efficiently remains a challenging task. Focusing on states with nonpositive partial transpose (NPT), we establish a hierarchy among entropy-based, majorization, realignment, and reduction criteria for Haar uniformly generated random states in finite dimensions, analyzing their performance based on rank and subsystem dimension. We prove lower bounds on the rank of mixed quantum states beyond which the realignment and entropic criteria fail to detect entanglement. We evaluate the relative effectiveness of the considered detection methods using three key indicators -- fraction of detected states, mean detectable entanglement, and minimum required entanglement. Our results provide insights into the entanglement thresholds needed for reliable detection, showing that, beyond a certain level of entanglement, all criteria become equally powerful for low-rank states, while a hierarchy emerges among the various criteria for moderate to high ranks. Intriguingly, the proposed ordering among the considered criteria in qubit-qudit systems is different from that in higher dimensions. Additionally, we establish that the detection efficiency is influenced by the asymmetry in the subsystem dimensions, by illustrating how the realignment criterion behaves more efficiently than other detection methods when the difference between the subsystem dimensions is small.
item.dc:creator: Akhil Kumar Awasthi, Sudipta Mondal, Rivu Gupta, Aditi Sen De

item.title: Work extraction from long-lived quantum coherence of a three-level system
item.description: arXiv:2508.02614v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze work-extraction protocols using the long-lived quantum coherence of a three-level quantum system coupled to a thermal bath. We identify conditions under which persistent quantum coherence can arise, i.e., for systems with degenerate excited states and aligned transition dipoles, or for nearly degenerate systems with small energy splittings. By proposing two thermodynamic protocols that employ energy-preserving unitary operations, we show that quantum coherence can be converted into population asymmetry, thereby serving as a quantum resource for work extraction. Specifically, we propose an optimized protocol to extract the maximum extractable work (MEW), measured by the free energy difference (FED), from quantum coherence in a single-shot thermodynamic cycle. Our results highlight the thermodynamic advantages of long-lived coherence in a three-level quantum system and could influence future designs of coherence-driven quantum thermal machines.
item.dc:creator: Wenjing Chen, Si-Wei Han, Ziye Wang, Xiaoshan Feng, Jun Feng

item.title: Lower-depth local encoding circuits for the surface code
item.description: arXiv:2509.09779v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The surface code is the most studied error-correcting code thanks to its high threshold, simple decoding, and locality in two dimensions (2D). A key component of any code is its encoding circuit, which maps an unencoded state to the corresponding encoded state. The best previous surface code encoding circuit compatible with 2D local connectivity requires depth $2d$ to encode distance-$d$ surface codes. This paper presents depth $d$ encoding circuits for the rotated surface code. Our circuit is constructed inductively from circuits that grow the code from $d$ to $(d+2)$. We prove that depth $d+O(1)$ is optimal for inductively constructed circuits.
item.dc:creator: Jahan Claes

item.title: Free mutual information and higher-point OTOCs
item.description: arXiv:2509.13406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a quantity called the free mutual information (FMI), adapted from concepts in free probability theory, as a new physical measure of quantum chaos. This quantity captures the spreading of a time-evolved operator in the space of all possible operators on the Hilbert space, which is doubly exponential in the number of degrees of freedom. It thus provides a finer notion of operator spreading than the well-understood phenomenon of operator growth in physical space. We derive two central results which apply in any physical system: first, an explicit "Coulomb gas" formula for the FMI of two observables $A(t)$ and $B$ in terms of the eigenvalues of the product operator $A(t)B$; and second, a general relation expressing the FMI as a weighted sum of all higher-point out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs). This second result provides a precise information-theoretic interpretation for the higher-point OTOCs as collectively quantifying operator ergodicity and the approach to freeness. This physical interpretation is particularly useful in light of recent progress in experimentally measuring higher-point OTOCs. We identify universal behaviours of the FMI and higher-point OTOCs across a variety of chaotic systems, including random unitary circuits and chaotic spin chains, which indicate that spreading in the doubly exponential operator space is a generic feature of quantum many-body chaos. At the same time, the non-generic behavior of the FMI in various non-chaotic systems, including certain unitary designs, shows that there are cases where an operator spreads in physical space but remains localized in operator space. The FMI is thus a sharper diagnostic of chaos than the standard 4-point OTOC.
item.dc:creator: Shreya Vardhan, Jinzhao Wang

item.title: Low Overhead Universal Quantum Computation with Triorthogonal Codes
item.description: arXiv:2510.05708v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the use of triorthogonal codes for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation and propose two methods to circumvent the Eastin-Knill theorem, which prohibits any single quantum error-correcting code from supporting both universality and a transversal gate set. We show that our methods reduce the resource overhead compared with existing fault-tolerant protocols. We develop a simple fault-tolerant implementation of the logical Hadamard gate for triorthogonal codes by exploiting the fact that they have transversal controlled-Z (CZ) gates, resulting in a circuit with reduced overhead. We also introduce a procedure for generating a symmetric Calderbank-Shor-Steane code paired with a triorthogonal code, which allows CNOT and CZ gate transversality across the pair of codes. In addition, we present logical state teleportation circuits that transfer encoded states between the two codes, allowing all logical operations to be performed transversally. Our methods can be integrated into the Steane error correction framework without incurring additional resource cost. Finally, using the 15-qubit code as an example, we demonstrate that our protocols significantly reduce the gate overhead compared with other existing methods. These results highlight the potential of combining distinct code structures to achieve low-overhead, universal fault-tolerant quantum computation.
item.dc:creator: Dawei Jiao, Mahdi Bayanifar, Alexei Ashikhmin, Olav Tirkkonen

item.title: Covariance and the use of the Schrodinger equation in quantum field theory
item.description: arXiv:2510.10333v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Schrodinger equation is not covariant. Nevertheless, quantum field theory is often formulated using the Schrodinger equation to describe the time evolution of the system, which is equivalent to using Feynman path integrals. It is well known that scattering theory gives covariant results provided that the interaction vanishes in the asymptotic limit of $t \rightarrow \pm \infty$, but there are other situations of interest that do not satisfy those conditions. As an example, the Aharonov-Bohm effect is derived here using second-quantized field theory to describe all the electrons as well as the electromagnetic field, which allows the effects of retarded vector potentials to be calculated in a straightforward way using the Feynman propagator. The results are in agreement with the usual expression for the Aharonov-Bohm effect when the retardation of the electromagnetic field is negligible, but they predict a fractional phase shift, a lack of covariance, and violations of causality when retardation effects are significant. These results suggest that quantum field theory based on the Schrodinger equation or Feynman path integrals is incomplete in the sense that it cannot give a correct description of all observable phenomena.
item.dc:creator: J. D. Franson

item.title: Hyperfine spectroscopy and nuclear spin control of dark defects in diamond
item.description: arXiv:2510.19598v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spin defects in diamond serve as powerful building blocks for quantum technologies, especially for quantum sensing and networking. Electron-nuclear defects formed near optically active spins such as the nitrogen-vacancy center provide a resource for multi-qubit quantum registers. However, many remain uncharacterized, limiting their control and integration in quantum devices. Here, we identify the hyperfine components, including their relative sign, and nuclear spin species of two unknown dark spin defects using zero-field double electron-electron resonance spectroscopy and a protocol based on electron-nuclear double resonance. New ab initio calculations assign one defect to a known nitrogen interstitial, while the hydrogen-related defect matches no calculated or previously reported structure. We further use this protocol to demonstrate initialization, unitary control, and long-lived coherence of the hydrogen nuclear spin qubit, with a coherence time of 1.0(3) ms. These characterization and control tools establish a framework for harnessing unknown electron-nuclear defects for quantum registers.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Ungar, Hao Tang, Andrew Stasiuk, Bo Xing, Boning Li, Ju Li, Alexandre Cooper, Paola Cappellaro

item.title: Sequential realization of Quantum Instruments
item.description: arXiv:2512.14588v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In adaptive quantum circuits classical results of mid-circuit measurements determine the upcoming gates. This allows POVMs, quantum channels or more generally quantum instruments to be implemented sequentially, so that fewer qubits need to be used at each of the $N$ measurement steps. In this paper, we mathematically describe these problems via adaptive sequence of instruments (ASI) and show how any instrument can be decomposed into it. Number of steps $N$ and number of ancillary qubits $n_A$ needed for actual implementation are crucial parameters of any such ASI. We show an achievable lower bound on the product $N.n_A$ and we determine in which situations this tradeoff is likely to be optimal. Contrary to common intuition we show that for quantum instruments which transform $n$ to $m(>n)$ qubits, there exist $N$-step ASI implementing them just with $(m-n)$ ancillary qubits, which are remeasured $(N-1)$ times and finally used as output qubits.
item.dc:creator: Soham Sau, Michal Sedl\'ak

item.title: Pervasive Vulnerability Analysis and Defense for QKD-based Quantum Private Query
item.description: arXiv:2601.01918v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum Private Query (QPQ) based on Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) is among the most practically viable quantum communication protocols, with application value second only to QKD itself. However, prevalent security vulnerabilities in the post-processing stages of most existing QKD-based QPQ protocols have been severely overlooked. This study focuses on hidden information extraction under undetermined signal bits, revealing that most such QPQ protocols face severe security threats even without complex quantum resources. Specifically, direct observation attack causes incremental information leakage, while the minimum error discrimination attack efficiently steals additional database inforamtion. To address these critical flaws, the proposed multi-encryption defense scheme is compatible with existing QPQ protocols. The study demonstrates the necessity of the multi-encryption strategy for the security of databases in QPQ, providing key theoretical and technical support for constructing practical QPQ protocols resistant to real-world attacks.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Peng, Bin Liu, JiaHao Huang, Nankun Mu, Wei Huang, Bingjie Xu, Fei Gao

item.title: Magnetic levitation and spatial superposition of a nanodiamond with a current-carrying chip
item.description: arXiv:2601.06608v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a current-carrying-chip scheme for generating spatial quantum superpositions using a levitating nanodiamond with a built-in nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre defect. Our setup is versatile, for a mass range of $10^{-19}~{\rm kg}\leq m\leq 10^{-17}~{\rm kg}$ a superposition size of range ${\cal O}(100){\rm nm} < \Delta x < {\cal O}(10) {\rm \mu m}$ is achievable in $t\leq 0.1$s, depending on the position we launch from the centre of the diamagnetic trap. Using numerical simulations, we provide an in-depth analysis of the chip that can support stable trapping of the particle in all three dimensions as well as create a spatial superposition along the $x$-axis, while producing a very tight trap in the transverse directions. This setup enables the creation of a Schr\"odinger cat state with a diamagnetically levitated nanoparticle in a table-top experiment. Although the mass and superposition size considered here remain below those required for a QGEM test, the proposed device provides a building block toward future QGEM experiments.
item.dc:creator: Qian Xiang, Shafaq Gulzar Elahi, Andrew Geraci, Sougato Bose, Anupam Mazumdar

item.title: Madelung hydrodynamics of spin-orbit coupling: action principles, currents, and correlations
item.description: arXiv:2601.10698v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We exploit the variational and Hamiltonian structures of quantum hydrodynamics with spin to unfold the correlation and torque mechanisms accompanying spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in electronic motion. Using Hamilton's action principle for the Pauli equation, we isolate SOC-induced quantum forces that act on the orbital Madelung--Bohm trajectories and complement the usual force terms known to appear in quantum hydrodynamics with spin. While the latter spin-hydrodynamic forces relate to the quantum geometric tensor (QGT), SOC-induced orbital forces originate from a particular current operator that contributes prominently to the spin current. This distinction between force terms reveals two fundamentally different mechanisms generating quantum spin-orbit correlations. Leveraging the Hamiltonian structure of the hydrodynamic system, we also elucidate spin transport features such as the correlation-induced quantum torques and the current shift in the spin Hall effect. This Hall shift leads to a new definition of the transport spin current thereby addressing an open question in spintronics. Finally, we illustrate the framework via the Madelung--Rashba equations for planar SOC configurations and propose a particle closure for possible numerical implementations.
item.dc:creator: Cesare Tronci

item.title: A Stochastic Reconstruction of Entangled States: from Quantum Foundations to Machine Learning and Decision Making
item.description: arXiv:2601.17070v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This article presents a concrete mathematical framework for the generation of entangled quantum states from classical stochastic processes. We demonstrate that any density operator $\rho_{AB}$ of a composite system can be derived from the correlations between two underlying stochastic processes, $X(t)$ and $Y(t)$, representing the random fluctuations of its subsystems. This construction utilizes a two-scale temporal scheme - micro and macro time - where quantum correlations emerge as macro-correlations derived from underlying micro-correlations. We propose the Double Covariance Model (DCM), which reproduces the some properties of quantum theory by treating quantum states as the fourth-order moment structure of an underlying classical probability space. DCM may also have potential implications for applications, particularly in quantum-inspired simulation and technology, and quantum-like modeling of cognition and decision making, as a tool for generation of density matrices with classical stochastic processes.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Khrennikov, Irina Basieva

item.title: Spectral Codes: A Geometric Formalism for Quantum Error Correction
item.description: arXiv:2601.19765v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a new geometric perspective on quantum error correction based on spectral triples in noncommutative geometry. In this approach, quantum error correcting codes are reformulated as low energy spectral projections of Dirac type operators that separate global logical degrees of freedom from local, correctable errors. Locality, code distance, and the Knill Laflamme condition acquire a unified spectral and geometric interpretation in terms of the induced metric and spectrum of the Dirac operator. Within this framework, a wide range of known error correcting codes including classical linear codes, stabilizer codes, GKP type codes, and topological codes are recovered from a single construction. This demonstrates that classical and quantum codes can be organized within a common geometric language. A central advantage of the spectral triple perspective is that the performance of error correction can be directly related to spectral properties. We show that leakage out of the code space is controlled by the spectral gap of the Dirac operator, and that code preserving internal perturbations can systematically increase this gap without altering the encoded logical subspace. This yields a geometric mechanism for enhancing error correction thresholds, which we illustrate explicitly for a stabilizer code. We further interpret Berezin Toeplitz quantization as a mixed spectral code and briefly discuss implications for holographic quantum error correction. Overall, our results suggest that quantum error correction can be viewed as a universal low energy phenomenon governed by spectral geometry.
item.dc:creator: Satoshi Kanno, Yoshi-aki Shimada

item.title: Entanglement in quantum spin chains is strictly finite at any temperature
item.description: arXiv:2602.13386v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Entanglement is the hallmark of quantum physics, yet its characterization in interacting many-body systems at thermal equilibrium remains one of the most important challenges in quantum statistical physics. We prove that the Gibbs state of any quantum spin chain can be exactly decomposed into a mixture of matrix product states with a bond dimension that is independent of the system size, at any nonzero temperature. As a consequence, the Schmidt number, arguably the most stringent measure of bipartite entanglement, is strictly finite for thermal states, even in the thermodynamic limit. Our decomposition is explicit and is accompanied by an efficient classical algorithm to sample the resulting matrix product states.
item.dc:creator: Ainesh Bakshi, Soonwon Choi, Sa\'ul Pilatowsky-Cameo

item.title: High-fidelity non-adiabatic dark state gates for neutral atoms
item.description: arXiv:2602.13885v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rydberg blockade gates are the most experimentally mature entangling operations in neutral-atom quantum processors, combining fast gate times with simple control, but their performance degrades at larger interatomic separations and remains sensitive to motional and technical noise. Non-blockade gate schemes, such as dark state and geometric protocols, offer complementary robustness but typically rely on complex and experimentally demanding control. Here we show that quantum optimal control enables non-blockade gate schemes to be implemented using the experimentally established pulse-shaping techniques developed for blockade-based gates. Focusing on the dark state gate, we construct non-adiabatic implementations that preserve the intrinsic robustness of adiabatic dark state protocols while achieving gate times comparable to time-optimal blockade gates using only smooth, experimentally feasible pulses. The resulting gates exhibit enhanced resilience to motional coupling, laser noise, and interaction inhomogeneity, particularly near and beyond the blockade radius. This work establishes a practical route to fast, robust non-blockade-based two-qubit gates without increased experimental complexity.
item.dc:creator: Nader Mostaan, Kapil Goswami, Peter Schmelcher, Rick Mukherjee

item.title: Quantum tomography for non-iid sources
item.description: arXiv:2602.22057v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum state and process tomography are typically analyzed under the assumption that devices emit independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) states or channels. In realistic experiments, however, noise, drift, feedback, or adaptive behavior can violate this assumption. We show that projected least-squares tomography remains statistically optimal even under fully adaptive state and channel preparation. Specifically, we prove that the sample complexity for reconstructing the time-averaged state or channel matches the optimal i.i.d. scaling up to logarithmic factors for non-adaptive, single-copy measurements. For average states of rank $r$, the sample complexity is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d r^2/\epsilon^2)$ to achieve trace-norm accuracy $\epsilon$, while for process tomography it is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^6/\epsilon^2)$ to achieve diamond-norm accuracy $\epsilon$. Thus, dropping the i.i.d.\ assumption does not increase the fundamental sample complexity of quantum tomography, but only changes the interpretation of the reconstructed object. Finally, by tracking the drift of the source using only past outcomes, we certify high average preparation purity and entanglement even when the time-averaged state is mixed or separable.
item.dc:creator: Leonardo Zambrano

item.title: Control of Multipartite Entanglement through Anisotropy against Thermal Noise
item.description: arXiv:2602.22815v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Preserving multipartite entanglement in open many-body quantum systems is fundamentally limited by unavoidable environmental noise. We study the open-system dynamics of multipartite entanglement in an anisotropic XXZ spin chain interacting with a thermal spin bath, focusing on two states with distinct types of multipartite entanglement: the generalized GHZ and the generalized W state. Using a master-equation approach combined with the Bethe ansatz technique, we show analytically that robustness of multipartite entanglement at low temperatures can be enhanced by suitably tuning the anisotropy of the system. Our results highlight interaction-induced spectral control as a mechanism for stabilizing multipartite entanglement in quantum computing platforms.
item.dc:creator: Samudra Sur, Saikat Sur

item.title: Unified Probe of Quantum Chaos and Ergodicity from Hamiltonian Learning
item.description: arXiv:2603.04486v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Developing measures of quantum ergodicity and chaos stands as a foundational task in the study of quantum many-body systems. In this work, we propose metrics for these effects based on Hamiltonian learning that unify multiple advantages of existing metrics. In particular, we show how ergodicity and chaos improve the robustness of Hamiltonian learning to small errors and furthermore demonstrate that this robustness can be used as a metric for such phenomena. We analytically and numerically show that our metrics not only distinguish between integrable and ergodic regimes in various spin chains but also quantify chaos and ergodicity, allowing us to locate regions of parameter space displaying maximal ergodicity and maximal sensitivity to local perturbations. Our approach not only provides conceptual ways to study quantum chaos and ergodicity but also presents viable experimental methods for quantum simulators.
item.dc:creator: Nik O. Gjonbalaj, Christian Kokail, Susanne F. Yelin, Soonwon Choi

item.title: Testing the 3D QRNG by Undoing
item.description: arXiv:2604.12724v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a method to test whether a photonic 3D QRNG operates according to the underlying theory by realizing the proposed measurement with the correct output probabilities and value-indefiniteness conditions, thereby generating strongly incomputable and maximally unpredictable sequences of random digits. The test relies on undoing the unitary evolution realized by the 3D QRNG. The test verifies the unitarity of the realized transformation, quantifies the magnitude of the residual noise, and detects those fabrication errors that are not common to the device and the undoing procedure; photon loss and dark counts are removed beforehand by heralding and are therefore outside its scope. By testing the validity of the implementation, the test can corroborate the theoretically proven features of the 3D QRNG, such as strong incomputability and unpredictability, or indicate how the implementation should be corrected, if necessary. The test can be easily incorporated into the QRNG and used as a means of experimental certification. The test module is fabricated identically to the QRNG.
item.dc:creator: J. M. Ag\"uero Trejo, Cristian S. Calude, O. C. Stoica

item.title: Quantum algorithm for solving high-dimensional linear stochastic differential equations via amplitude encoding of the noise term
item.description: arXiv:2604.24133v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work studies quantum algorithms to solve high-dimensional stochastic differential equations (SDEs) $\mathrm{d} \mathbf{X}_t = A(t) \mathbf{X}_t \mathrm{d} t + B(t) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{W}_t$. Aiming for a speed-up in the dimension $N$ of $\mathbf{X}_t$, we generate quantum states that encode $\mathbf{X}_t$ in the amplitudes, while most of the existing quantum methods for SDEs employ binary encoding. A key challenge is the amplitude encoding of the noise term, and we address this by utilizing the quantum circuit implementation of a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG). We propose two methods: the Dyson series-based method and the Euler-Maruyama (EM)-based method. In the former, we express the noise term via the Dyson series approximation of the time evolution operator, while in the latter, it is approximated using the EM time discretization. Both methods use the quantum linear systems solver to generate the amplitude-encoding state of $\mathbf{X}_t$, making only ${\rm polylog}(N)$ queries to the PRNG circuit and the block-encodings of $A$ and $B$. Additionally, going beyond state preparation, we present methods to estimate expectations of functions of $\mathbf{X}_t$ using the state.
item.dc:creator: Koichi Miyamoto

item.title: Quantum Proper Scoring Rules: Convex Duality, Bregman Risk, and the Coherence Gap
item.description: arXiv:2605.05268v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We generalize proper scoring rules to the quantum domain, replacing probability distributions with density operators. We define Quantum Value Functionals via convex generators and establish a duality theory yielding proper quantum scoring rules using McCarthy's tangent-plane construction. We derive local minimax optimal bounds for quantum state tomography under these incentives, proving a Local Holevo-McCarthy Bound that explicitly links asymptotic risk to the Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori metric and the Holevo bound. Furthermore, we establish an exact coherence floor that quantifies the irreducible excess score of fixed-basis forecasting strategies when phases are unknown (minimax over the phase orbit), proving a worst-case minimax floor of $\log d$ over the full state space. Our results contextualize fundamental sample complexity separations compared to optimal quantum estimation strategies and guide the design of incentive-compatible quantum data markets and robust quantum machine learning protocols.
item.dc:creator: M. W. AlMasri

item.title: Quantum circuit design via dynamic Pauli constraints
item.description: arXiv:2605.22744v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce the Motte model, a software-oriented model of quantum computation motivated by the practical constraints of near-term quantum hardware. In this model, gates are specified by constraints expressed in terms of Pauli observables, with each disjoint layer of gates accompanied by a pairwise or k-local quantum state tomography of the device. We prove that the model is equivalent to the coupling-graph-restricted circuit model, and hence universal for BQP, with only polynomial overhead: emulating a depth-D circuit on N qubits requires O(D^2 N log N) elementary operations. Because the gate applied at each step is fixed exactly by the tomographic report, this emulation is robust to both the sampling and readout noise of the tomography. The model formalizes an idiom shared by existing work that ranges from quantum imaginary time evolution for the study of quantum systems to the use of quantum computers for procedural generation in games. It therefore provides a natural interface for designing quantum software entirely in terms of physically observable quantities, relevant for the NISQ era and into fault-tolerance, with gate and decoherence noise lying outside the present scope.
item.dc:creator: James R. Wootton, Merlin Incerti-Medici, Daniel Bultrini, Pierre Fromholz

item.title: Classical State Preparation for Variational Quantum Algorithms via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2605.23138v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) potentially offer a pathway to practical quantum advantage, but their optimization is heavily hindered by barren plateaus and numerous local minima. While classically simulable Clifford circuits can warm-start VQAs to accelerate convergence, existing heuristic-based initialization methods struggle to scale within vast combinatorial search spaces. We address this bottleneck with CRiSP (a Clifford Reinforcement Learning agent for State Preparation), which casts Clifford prefix selection as a sequential decision-making problem. CRiSP utilizes Neural-Guided Monte Carlo Tree Search, driven by a Transformer-based policy trained via self-play, to insert learned Clifford gates before fixed parameterized rotations. This enables the construction of high-quality initial states entirely through polynomial-time classical stabilizer simulation. By integrating a curriculum learning strategy that progressively expands the search horizon, the agent efficiently scales to deep circuits. Evaluated on QAOA benchmarks of up to $22$ qubits and $1{,}370$ parameters, CRiSP outperforms state-of-the-art Clifford initialization methods by a mean of $3.19\times$ (max $45.02\times$) in average energy accuracy and $2.41\times$ (max $16.01\times$) in best-achieved energy accuracy. Assessments on VQE tasks further demonstrate the framework's robustness and generalizability.
item.dc:creator: Gino Kwun, Dhanvi Bharadwaj, Gokul Subramanian Ravi

item.title: How to make quantum cheese: efficient geometry oracles for exponentially many pseudorandom microstructures
item.description: arXiv:2606.00222v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum algorithms for partial differential equations often assume oracle access to the geometry of the material being simulated. As explicitly specifying a geometry pixel by pixel on an exponentially large grid automatically yields an exponential cost, a central question is when such oracles can effectively be implemented by polynomially sized quantum circuits. We give explicit polynomial-size circuits for a family of geometries with exponentially many pseudorandom microscopic features. The geometry is generated by a pseudorandom procedure and a convolution with a local kernel to shape the texture. This proves to be a versatile framework, that includes materials with fixed-shape holes, spatially correlated textures, and activation--inhibition patterns. For a fixed kernel with bounded integer coefficients, the oracle cost is polynomial in the number of qubits, even when the number of microfeatures is exponential. We implement the circuit constructions in PsiQuantum Construct and verify their behaviour through numerical simulation. We also discuss why efficient access does not follow from an arbitrary description of the material, by proving worst-case query lower bounds for amplitude-encoded formation fields and databases of holes.
item.dc:creator: Alice Barthe

item.title: Mach's principle in atomic transitions
item.description: arXiv:2606.11608v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the atomic transition probabilities in atom-mirror set-ups that are in circular motion. In one scenario, the atom is in circular motion inside a static cylindrical mirror. In the other scenario, the cylindrical mirror rotates around its central axis while the atom remains static. We report structural similarity in the atomic transition probabilities between these two cases -- these probabilities are equivalent upon interchanging the field frequencies between the two scenarios. We interpret such an observation as a semi-classical phenomenon analogous to the classical Mach's principle.
item.dc:creator: Subhajit Barman, Bibhas Ranjan Majhi

item.title: Local correlations in long-range dual-unitary kicked Hamiltonian chains
item.description: arXiv:2606.13857v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many-body Floquet models with exact space--time duality, such as the kicked Ising chain, provide paradigmatic examples of dual-unitary dynamics. The requirement of exact space--time duality is, however, highly restrictive and, in its standard formulation, permits only nearest-neighbor interactions. We demonstrate that the latter constraint can be avoided, still resulting in exactly solvable models. In particular, we construct a broad class of dual-unitary kicked spin chains with long-range interactions. We show that, for an interaction range $r$, local two-point connected correlation functions propagate along the edges of the light cone, $|n|=r|t|$, and can be evaluated analytically for local observables. We illustrate our general statement by analytic calculation of the connected correlation function for a kicked Ising chain with next-to-next-nearest-neighbor interactions.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Al. Osipov, Marc Cedric Spyra, Jana Carolina Schumann, Thomas Guhr, Boris Gutkin

item.title: The use of Peres lattices in periodically driven systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.20009v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We demonstrate the strength of the method of Peres lattices in periodically driven quantum systems. The method, which has previously been used mostly in stationary systems, enables us to efficiently detect resonances in the driven system, to monitor the onset of chaos, and to recognize critical properties of the Floquet modes. It also allows quick comparisons of the spectra of Floquet modes for various driving Hamiltonians and transparent tests of the iterative approximation techniques based on effective stationary Hamiltonians.
item.dc:creator: Luk\'a\v{s} Honsa, Jan St\v{r}ele\v{c}ek, Jakub Novotn\'y, Pavel Cejnar

item.title: Context-Verified, Error-Budget-Aware Decomposition Selection for Toffoli Networks
item.description: arXiv:2606.31791v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The cheapest Toffoli (CCX) decompositions (relative-phase and control-reduced Toffolis) save two-qubit gates, which dominate the error budget of near-term hardware, but they are correct only in context, since a relative phase is observable only when superposed branches interfere. We propose quantum chip performance tuning (QCPT), a compiler that selects the cheapest decomposition for each Toffoli (stage 1) and admits it only if a per-instance check shows that it equals the exact gate, up to one phase, on every state that can enter it; a whole-circuit certificate gates the output. The output acts as the exact circuit on every valid input, superposed ones included, up to a reported global phase, which per-state checks do not guarantee. Substituting relative-phase Toffolis wherever they fit changes the unitary of six of twelve benchmark circuits used as subroutines, whereas stage 1 changes none and removes 31.0% of the two-qubit gates. A certified resynthesis of classical circuits of up to ten qubits raises the saving to 43.1% on the primary suite and to 57.5% on 20 small RevLib circuits (in-sample). A bound on the compilation error plus the per-gate device error separates what the compiler adds from what a depolarizing two-qubit model of the device adds. In mirror tests on ibm_aachen, QCPT (best of four candidates, one of them the Qiskit circuit) returns more often than Qiskit on all nine circuits; in simulation with the calibration that drives its selection, on 29 of 33 circuits and worse on none by more than 0.01. An iterative language-model search with our certificate obtains no fewer gates on any of nine circuits and needs about 45 times longer (one run each). QCPT gives no gain without Toffoli structure. Certified context-dependent selection can thus let near-term devices run larger Toffoli circuits at a given success probability, with a gain that varies by family.
item.dc:creator: Karol Bartkiewicz, Patrycja Tulewicz

item.title: A Single Physical Principle Determines Quantum Relative Entropy
item.description: arXiv:2607.01712v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Why does quantum relative entropy occupy such a privileged role among measures of distinguishability? We show that a single operational principle determines it. If one pair of states can be distinguished at least as successfully as another for every prior, when both are assisted by the same auxiliary pair, acting as a catalyst, a distinguishability measure should assign it no smaller value. Remarkably, for a normalized measure, this requirement singles out Umegaki relative entropy under mild classical continuity and expansibility on uniform distributions: adding impossible outcomes leaves their associated entropy unchanged. Qubit catalysts already suffice. No additivity or quantum continuity is assumed. We also prove that, without auxiliary assistance, respecting binary discrimination dominance uniquely determines the quantum extension of every regular classical divergence, including the Hirche--Tomamichel extensions of classical $f$-divergences. For additive classical divergences, these extensions respect classical catalysis; allowing noncommuting qubit catalysts is what singles out Umegaki relative entropy.
item.dc:creator: Gilad Gour

item.title: Quantum linear solvers for quantum chemistry: prospects of exponential quantum advantage
item.description: arXiv:2607.08220v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum linear solvers (QLSs) offer the potential for quantum advantage in solving quantum chemical problems, but assessing such an advantage hinges on determining condition number ($\kappa$) scaling, which itself is computationally challenging. While a recent work applied the HHL algorithm to single-reference linearized coupled cluster (SRLCC), the validity of the framework is restricted to weakly correlated regimes. We thus begin by extending QLS-SRLCC to its multi-reference form, the internally contracted multi-reference LCC (QLS-icMRLCC). We then analyze $\kappa$ scaling across a diverse range of systems as well as bases in both QLS-SRLCC and QLS-icMRLCC, using three complementary diagnostics that range from explicit computations to use of indirect structural indicators: (i) direct calculations of $\kappa$, (ii) scaling of the ratio of maximum to minimum diagonal entries of an $A$ matrix, and (iii) structural analyses of the $A$ matrices based on a recently proposed conjecture that we adapt to the QLS-LCC problem. The three approaches yield broadly consistent predictions, with our numerical results indicating a slow-growing $\kappa$ scaling in system size for the sampled systems. For icMRLCC, however, the observed behaviour depends on the reference active space, leaving the broader prospects of quantum advantage with it less certain. This finding, when combined with our arguments on sub-linear scaling of sparsity (when excitation rank>2), supports the prospects of exponential advantage for QLS-LCC. However, the prospects of a QLS-level advantage do not necessarily translate to a speed-up in an end-to-end workflow. Finally, up to 28-qubit HHL-icMRLCCSD numerical calculations on potential energy curves of model systems containing up to four atoms recover the ground state energies with about $0.012\%$ errors relative to benchmark classical methods.
item.dc:creator: Peniel Bertrand Tsemo, Kenji Sugisaki, Ishita Bhattacharjee, V. S. Prasannaa

item.title: Entanglement entropy in two-particle Grover walks on graphs
item.description: arXiv:2607.09066v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We define a two-particle quantum walk of identical particles on a graph $G$ via the one-particle Grover walk on the Kronecker product $G \otimes G$, and call it the two-particle Grover walk. In systems of identical particles, quantum mechanics requires that quantum states have a certain invariance with respect to the exchange of particles. Focusing on the symmetry of the Kronecker product $G \otimes G$ as a graph, we show that the time evolution operator of this walk commutes with the swap operator, which ensures that this requirement is satisfied. Furthermore, we study the entanglement entropy of quantum states evolved by this walk. For the complete bipartite graph $K_{n,n}$, we completely determine the values of $n$ for which the quantum states evolved from specific initial states attain the upper bound of the entropy at some time, and prove that they are exactly $1$ and $2$.
item.dc:creator: Sho Kubota, Haruhiko Matsubara, Etsuo Segawa

item.title: Geometric Mode Steering of the Quantum Mpemba Effect
item.description: arXiv:2607.14501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The slowest Liouvillian mode often bottlenecks the relaxation of an open quantum system to its steady state. Standard strategies circumvent this bottleneck by selecting special initial states or engineering the dissipator. Here we investigate this problem when the input and the subsequent dissipative generator are prescribed. We introduce a predissipative geometric steering protocol that reshapes a prescribed pure or mixed state before relaxation begins---coherent rotations interleaved with nonselective projective measurements---at a fixed Lindblad generator. By steering the state's Bloch direction along geodesic paths, the protocol suppresses its overlap with the slowest Liouvillian modes. The prepared state can then start farther from equilibrium yet relax faster, realizing the quantum Mpemba effect, as diagnosed by reduced slow-mode overlap and a larger initial distance to stationarity, with distance crossings for complex slow modes verified from the full dynamics. Our framework treats real and complex spectral gaps within a common mode-overlap description. We also quantify the state-side cost of this preparation through cumulative measurement-induced mixing and illustrate its tradeoff with fidelity for a mixed target. We demonstrate Mpemba acceleration in driven qubit and multiqubit systems and discuss the required operations in trapped-ion and superconducting platforms.
item.dc:creator: Yingying Hong, Longxing Xu, Weiwei Zhang, Jie Ren, Jianhui Wang

item.title: Quantum error-correcting codes from aperiodic monotiles: the Hat and the Spectre
item.description: arXiv:2607.15326v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Li and Boyle showed that the Penrose tiling defines a quantum error-correcting code: superpositions of tilings over isometry orbits protect quantum information against erasure of any bounded region. We extend the construction to the aperiodic monotiles discovered by Smith, Myers, Kaplan and Goodman-Strauss. For the Hat, we prove strong local indistinguishability for all Hat tilings, and we prove local recoverability unconditionally for all nonsingular Hat tilings via the torus parametrization of the underlying cut-and-project scheme. The remaining singular case reduces to one sharply posed geometric question -- can a region that is a union of hats be retiled a second way? -- which we verify computationally has no counterexample up to a substantial scale: a certified $2490$-tile patch admits precisely one tiling by hats, so all $2^{2490}$ of its tile-subregions retile uniquely. Unlike the Penrose, Ammann-Beenker and Fibonacci tilings, both monotiles form two local-indistinguishability classes, so their code spaces split into two erasure-correcting sectors carrying a superselected classical label. Whether the label survives depends on which isometries are gauged: the Spectre's classes are exchanged by a $30^{\circ}$ rotation and merge once all proper isometries are gauged, whereas the Hat's are exchanged only by reflections. Under the physically natural gauge group $SE(2)$, the Hat code therefore stores one robust classical bit -- the handedness of its long-range order, readable in any bounded window with separation $\Delta = |K|\sqrt{5}/3$ -- alongside its protected quantum sectors. It is the reflexible monotile, not the chiral one, that carries the chirality bit. We give the exact Perron-Frobenius data of both codes, including the per-class reflected-Hat frequencies $(3\mp\sqrt{5})/6$ and the Spectre orientation-class frequencies $(5\pm\sqrt{15})/10$.
item.dc:creator: Josep Batle, Adam Bednorz

item.title: Machine-Learned Compact Subspace Generation for Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction within Density Matrix Embedding Framework
item.description: arXiv:2607.20585v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), an extension of quantum selected configuration interaction (QSCI), is a promising hybrid quantum-classical paradigm for molecular ground-state energies. By replacing variational optimization with quantum sampling, QSCI avoids barren plateaus and directly reconstructs correlated wavefunctions. However, existing configuration recovery mainly enforces symmetry constraints without targeting the most physically relevant configurations, often yielding oversized subspaces and costly classical diagonalization. We introduce QSCI-RBM, a compact subspace generation protocol based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), and integrate it within Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET). The RBM learns the distribution of dominant determinants from hardware samples, generating high-probability configurations. Sampling was performed on IBM Heron R1 (\texttt{ibm\_torino}) for CH$_5$NO, R2 (\texttt{ibm\_fez}) for C$_2$H$_4$, and R3 (\texttt{ibm\_boston}) for the larger H$_2$O benchmark and the protein-ligand system. After validating on these benchmarks of increasing active-space size, we simulate the inhibitor Carmofur bound to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (M\textsuperscript{pro}), fragmented into ten DMET impurities. Both DMET-QSCI-RBM and a DMET-SQD baseline reach chemical-potential self-consistency within four $\mu$-iterations. At the converged chemical potential, DMET-QSCI-RBM lies within $0.05\,\mathrm{mHa}$ of DMET-FCI while accessing on average only $0.22\%$ of the symmetry-preserving configuration space, versus $0.55\,\mathrm{mHa}$ at $33.0\%$ for DMET-SQD, leading to a $\sim$153-fold subspace reduction. RBM-assisted expansion thus yields far more compact hardware-derived determinant spaces at equal or better accuracy, reducing classical overhead for scalable quantum embedding of biological systems on real hardware.
item.dc:creator: Ashish Kumar Patra, Anurag K. S. V., Ruchika Bhat, Sai Shankar P., Rahul Maitra, Jaiganesh G

item.title: Random unitary circuits with constant spectral gap
item.description: arXiv:2607.20919v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove constant lower bounds for the spectral gap of the following random walks on unitary groups $\mathsf{SU}(2^n)$ on $n$ qubits. (i) Random Pauli Rotation: choose an $n$-qubit Pauli operator $P$ and an angle $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$, both uniformly at random, and apply $e^{\mathrm i \theta P}$. (ii) Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit: choose $n-1$ unitaries $U_{i}$ uniformly at random from $\mathsf{SU}(4)$ (including central phases of the parent group) independently, and apply $U_{2j-1}$ on two qubits $2j-1, 2j$ and then $U_{2j}$ on two qubits $2j, 2j+1$. Importantly, the gap bounds are independent of $n$ and apply for all finite dimensional unitary representations of $\mathsf{SU}(2^n)$ uniformly. Our results immediately imply that the Random Pauli Rotation and Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit converge to approximate unitary $t$-designs after $\mathcal{O}(nt)$ steps. As a consequence, we improve implications for the complexity growth of random unitary circuits as a function of the depth. The existing argument can be applied almost verbatim, but previously the depth had to be $\mathcal{O}(2^{cn})$ for some $c < 1$. Our unconditional constant spectral gap removes this restriction. We prove analogous constant-gap results for orthogonal and Clifford groups; the latter is indispensable for our result on the Brickwork Random Unitary Circuit. The former implies convergence to approximate orthogonal $t$-designs. In this case, the implied mixing time with respect to a constant additive and multiplicative error is optimal (up to an absolute constant factor) for $t=2$.
item.dc:creator: Tim Baer, Jeongwan Haah

item.title: A Bohmian version of a 2-state quantum system
item.description: arXiv:2607.24480v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: I construct a Bohmian version of a 2-state quantum system, where in addition to the quantum state, the system is characterized by a definite physical state which changes stochastically under the guidance of the quantum state. I argue that the probabilities produced by this process are well-defined, contrary to claims in "Why quantum mechanics cannot be formulated as a Markov process" by D. Gillespie (1994) about a related model.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Dickau

item.title: Noise-robust discrimination of incoherent point sources with spatial-mode demultiplexing
item.description: arXiv:2608.01765v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We theoretically predict and experimentally demonstrate that a reduced spatial-mode demultiplexing (SPADE) measurement using only the two lowest-order Hermite-Gaussian modes exhibits remarkable robustness against background noise in discriminating between a single source and two incoherent point sources. We establish a theoretical framework incorporating uniform background noise and derive an analytical Chernoff exponent expression, showing that SPADE consistently outperforms direct imaging (DI) across all source separations. Experimental results confirm that SPADE-based hypothesis testing approaches the quantum limit even when the background-to-signal photon ratio per pixel is 0.11. This advantage stems from SPADE's ability to concentrate source information into minimal detection modes, reducing the cumulative background noise impact. Our findings provide a practical detection scheme for applications where background noise is inevitable, such as astronomical observations and quantum sensing.
item.dc:creator: Jian-Qiang Liu, Chao-Ning Hu, Jun Xin, Xiao-Ming Lu

item.title: Is the Quantum-Entangled Universe a Small World?
item.description: arXiv:2608.19459v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Partial entanglement may provide enough connections in the universe to satisfy the definition of a small world. To investigate this possibility, we define a network of particles on a given space-like hyper-surface with a long-range link between any two particles that are connected by a chain of exchanged particles involving a limited number of interactions. Considering the mean free paths of particles in different regions of space and the resulting probability distributions of entanglement connections vs. distance, we find evidence of small-world or random network structure on all but the smallest scales - corresponding to stars and planets - on which other types of connections would need to be added to complete the small world picture.
item.dc:creator: Gregory S. Duane

item.title: Decay versus dephasing in Rydberg analog optimization: the exchange rate depends on the readout
item.description: arXiv:2608.29858v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Numerical studies of noisy Rydberg-atom optimization compress decoherence into a single rate, treating spontaneous decay ($\Gamma$) and dephasing ($\gamma$) as equivalent. We resolve the two as independent Lindblad axes for quantum annealing of unit-disk maximum independent set at fixed annealing time and ask how their relative effect depends on the readout. For the raw readout the size error collapses onto the effective dephasing rate $u=\kappa\Gamma+\gamma$, and at small noise a unit of decay rate degrades the result as much as $\kappa=7.4$ units of dephasing rate; a collapse fit across the whole grid returns 8.3. After greedy completion followed by a $(1,2)$-swap local search, classical post-processing of polynomial cost, the exchange rate falls to $\kappa=1.6$, and at the calibrated operating point of a commercial device dephasing produces three quarters of the noise-induced error instead of two fifths. First-order perturbation theory built from noiseless propagation gives the decay and dephasing susceptibilities of every readout, raw or post-processed, to a few parts in $10^6$ of the full Lindblad result. The raw asymmetry is set at the end of the schedule, where a decay event deletes an atom and a dephasing event leaves the readout unchanged. Post-processing refills most deletions and leaves misplaced atoms, which the two channels produce at comparable rates. Which channel limits a device therefore depends on the readout as well as on the hardware.
item.dc:creator: Seunghyeon Kim, Minjoo Kim, Junwoo Jung

item.title: Non-local Magic: closed-form solution and equivalence with magic of purification
item.description: arXiv:2609.04119v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Non-local magic quantifies the non-stabilizerness beyond the local choice of basis. Its evaluation is a hard problem requiring optimization over local unitaries. Here, we show that for the log-stabilizer fidelity this optimization admits an exact closed-form analytic solution depending only on the Schmidt spectrum. We then address the open problem of non-stabilizerness of mixed states by introducing the magic of purification and show that it naturally induces a resource theory whose free states are the states with zero stabilizer entropy. For the log-stabilizer fidelity, the magic of purification admits a distance-based formulation in terms of the Uhlmann fidelity. We prove that non-local magic coincides with the minimum magic of purification along the unitary orbit of the reduced density operator. This framework introduces non-local magic as the relevant resource for non-trivial steering and the characterization of entangling and non-stabilizer resources in measurements. These results provide both an efficient analytical characterization and a mixed-state resource-theoretic interpretation of non-local magic.
item.dc:creator: Michele Viscardi, Lorenzo Leone, Alioscia Hamma

item.title: Photonic Time-Delayed Quantum Extreme Learning Machine
item.description: arXiv:2609.07416v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose and numerically simulate a photonic quantum extreme learning machine (QELM) based on non-linear interactions in a time-delay non-linear interferometer with photon-number-resolving detection. We theoretically demonstrate the QELM's computational capability by binary classification of the non-linear two moons benchmark. Analysis of the learned output weights and alternative quantum readouts shows that compact feature sets based on photon-number correlations preserve classification accuracy while potentially reducing measurement complexity. We further show that the QELM maintains its classification performance under the effect of losses by naturally redistributing the learned weights across a larger set of available features. These results highlight the potential of time-delay photonic implementation as an experimentally accessible QELM platform.
item.dc:creator: Ekaterina Protsenko, Caterina Vigliar, Francesco Da Ros

item.title: Predictive Structure Behind Rare Outcomes in Random Quantum Circuits
item.description: arXiv:2609.17482v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Local random quantum circuits can occasionally produce unusually large output probabilities. However, the final output distribution containing such a peak does not by itself reveal how the peak formed during circuit evolution. We investigate whether states formed during circuit evolution carry structural signatures that predict subsequent peak formation. In numerical experiments, circuits selected for large terminal peaks exhibit stronger pairwise correlations and probability redistribution, together with lower bipartite entanglement and output entropy, than controls generated by the same random-circuit model. Their intermediate states retain higher fresh-peak event probability when the remaining gates are independently regenerated. Within an unconditioned ensemble, a fixed structural score computed from the initial circuit segment predicts new-peak probability. Averaged equally across n=8-16, a replay with equal numbers of remaining-circuit evaluations shows that score-based allocation yields 1.80 times as many peaks as uniform allocation and about 18% more than a fixed baseline based on probability concentration and redistribution. Randomizing relative phases while preserving computational-basis probabilities strongly attenuates the selected-state advantage, demonstrating a functional contribution from relative-phase organization. Controlled gate-selection tests further show that the identified structure can guide circuit construction to promote peak formation. Together, these results connect rare output events to intermediate-state structure with predictive and constructive value under finite-depth local dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Myeongsu Kim, Travis Humble, Sabre Kais

item.title: Quantum Generative Modeling with a Coherent Memory, Exact Training and a Memory-Dimension Advantage
item.description: arXiv:2609.23050v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce the coherent memory Born machine (CoMB), an algorithm for quantum generative modeling on a register whose size does not depend on the dimension of the data. CoMB generates a sample one component per round. In each round, a work register is entangled with a memory register and measured, and the outcome gives one component. The memory is never measured and carries correlations between rounds. We show that the characteristic function of the generated distribution is a product of small matrices, one per round. This gives exact training, with maximum mean discrepancy losses and gradients costing time linear in the data dimension, without sampling or likelihood. We also compile every round onto one work qubit and evaluate device noise exactly. To isolate coherence, each CoMB is compared with its dephased twin and with equally trained classical hidden Markov models. We benchmark it on continuous data, $368$-cell calorimeter showers from five qubits, and on sequential data, handwritten digits from three qubits. The coherent memory provides a memory-dimension advantage. Four coherent levels do the work of about six classical states on both benchmarks, and of at least five with $95\%$ confidence on showers at every training budget, including convergence. On showers, removing their coherence raises the loss by $23$ to $31\%$. With eight levels, where all models approach a common floor, coherent and classical memories become indistinguishable with longer training. On an IBM Heron processor, the memory carries two thirds of the inter-round correlation through twelve mid-circuit measurements.
item.dc:creator: Jamal Slim. Saverio Monaco, Ran Xue, Dirk Kruecker, Kerstin Borras

item.title: Exponential Quantum Advantage in Testing Fourier Dimensionality
item.description: arXiv:2609.25816v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A boolean function $f$ has Fourier dimension $k$ if its strings with nonzero Fourier coefficients span a subspace of dimension $k$. We first consider the property testing task of determining whether a function has Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. We show that there is an $O(k/\sqrt{\epsilon})$-query quantum property tester for this problem, which we show to be almost optimal. Combined with Gopalan \etal's classical lower bound of $\Omega(2^{k/2})$, this demonstrates an exponential quantum advantage for this task. We complement this result with a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester, giving a quadratic improvement over the previous best tester, and essentially settling the classical query complexity. We then introduce and study the tolerant version of this problem. That is, determining whether a function is $\alpha\epsilon$-close to having Fourier dimension at most $k$, or is $\epsilon$-far from being so. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that this tolerant version of the problem is essentially just as hard as the standard version of the problem. That is, we show this problem has a $\tilde{O}(k/\epsilon)$ quantum tester, and a $\tilde{O}(2^{k/2}/\epsilon)$ classical tester.
item.dc:creator: Kenny Chen

item.title: Multipartite GHZ diagonal states and their entanglement properties
item.description: arXiv:2609.28351v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the family of GHZ diagonal states, which are mixed multipartite quantum states that are diagonal in a GHZ type basis. We show that the class of GHZ diagonal states is highly symmetric and exhibits rich entanglement properties, making it relevant for applications in multipartite quantum key distribution.
item.dc:creator: Luka Burduli, Johannes Moerland, Peter Schupp

item.title: Universal Inductive Inference of Quantum States
item.description: arXiv:2609.36912v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Solomonoff's universal inductive inference [Inf. Control. 1964] is one of the most general frameworks for learning from sequential data and predicting future observations. It provides prediction guarantees for any computable stochastic source. We ask whether an analogous universal theory of induction can be developed for quantum systems. To this end, we introduce universal quantum inductive inference, a framework for learning and predicting quantum sources that may exhibit arbitrary correlations and entanglement across time. Given the outcomes of past measurements and the corresponding post-measurement quantum systems, the learner produces a joint state that predicts the next measurement outcome and post-measurement system while preserving correlations with the past systems. We model a quantum source as a multipartite quantum state whose description is generated by an unknown $s$-bit program within a given time bound. The learner is required to produce a state that is $\epsilon$-close in trace distance to the target with probability at least $1-\delta$. We establish an information-theoretic inference algorithm with round complexity $O(s\epsilon^{-2}\delta^{-1})$. We further prove a matching lower bound in the relevant parameter regime, even for classical sources. As a second result, we construct a non-i.i.d. state tomography algorithm that outputs a classical description of the conditional state of the next system given past measurement outcomes. Our information-theoretic tomography algorithm achieves round complexity $O(sn^2\epsilon^{-4}\delta^{-2})$, where $n$ is the number of qubits received in each round. Finally, we investigate the computational hardness of universal quantum inductive inference under quantum cryptographic assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Taiga Hiroka, Min-Hsiu Hsieh, Yuki Shirakawa

item.title: A Tale of Two Walks: From Kac to KMP and Back
item.description: arXiv:2609.38044v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We reveal an unexpected connection between two interacting particle systems: Kac's walk and the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) process. We first establish a mixing-time analogue of Aldous's conjecture for the KMP process on general graphs: the mixing time of the $t$-particle process on any connected $d$-vertex graph is at most $O(\log d)$ times the corresponding single-particle mixing time, uniformly in $t$. As an application, we improve the mixing-time bound for coordinate hit-and-run on the $n$-dimensional standard simplex from $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ [KV26] to $O(n\log n)$, while removing the dependence on the initial distribution. We then show that the twirling channel induced by the parallel Kac's walk on the symmetric subspace can be exactly encoded by a Markov chain on partitions, which naturally lifts to a parallel KMP chain on the complete graph. We prove that $O(\log d+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ repetitions of the parallel Kac's walk suffice to approximate Haar twirling on the symmetric subspace of $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t}$ to error $\varepsilon$, uniformly in all $t$. Our main technical contribution is a new structural property of KMP-type dynamics: conditional product structure, which holds for both the standard KMP processes on general graphs and the parallel KMP processes on complete graphs. Conditioned on suitable auxiliary randomness, the evolution of the labeled KMP process factorizes into independent single-particle updates. Combining this structure with an exact coupling inspired by the analysis of Kac's walk, we remove the dependence on the number of particles from the mixing bounds for both unlabeled KMP models. This bypasses the $\log(\pi_{\min}^{-1})$ dependency from spectral-gap arguments, which is often prohibitively large for many-particle systems. Using this framework, we prove mixing bounds that are sharp up to logarithmic factors for both unlabeled KMP models.
item.dc:creator: Qian Chen, Jingcheng Liu, Minglong Qin, Leonard J. Schulman, Fang Song, Penghui Yao, Mingnan Zhao

item.title: Single-shot state preparation thresholds in quantum LDPC codes: soundness, confinement, and statistical mechanics
item.description: arXiv:2609.39965v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Single-shot error correction does not by itself establish equally direct and robust logical-state initialization. We study preparation of CSS quantum low-density parity-check code states using one noisy round of the code's checks. We prove that linear confinement over a weight range growing at least logarithmically, together with at least logarithmic distance, suffices for a nonzero threshold under independent local-stochastic readout and data noise in the relevant CSS sector. The threshold is certified by ideal recovery of a decoder-defined logical channel. The key is a correction rule that preserves the logical class under local syndrome changes, allowing the proof to proceed without a local-stochastic bound on the preparation residual. This gives a single-block guarantee for quantum expander codes without dimension jumps or batching. Under the stronger linear-soundness hypothesis, we establish local-stochastic residual noise, enabling composition with compatible fault-tolerant gadgets. For a retained-record formulation, we also derive an exact statistical-mechanical representation of optimal final recovery at fixed preparation decoder. A decoder-dependent logical-sector order parameter characterizes asymptotically successful block decoding. Monte Carlo results for the three-dimensional toric code provide finite-size evidence for a threshold beyond both linear sufficient conditions. These results distinguish logical robustness from local-stochastic residual-noise control and identify decoder consistency as a route to single-shot initialization.
item.dc:creator: Yuanchen Zhao, Yi Yuan, Zhengyi Han, Dong E. Liu

item.title: Computational Bounds for $f$-Routing
item.description: arXiv:2609.40278v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The $f$-routing protocol is a leading candidate for quantum position verification (Kent, Munro, and Spiller, Physical Review A, 2011), but security guarantees for explicit functions remain limited. We prove unconditional resource lower bounds for uniform attackers. Our techniques bypass communication-complexity bounds central to previous works, which are inherently at most linear in the input length. We show that, for input length $n$ and a sufficiently small constant $\epsilon>0$, a uniform strategy running in time $T$ and succeeding with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ on every input implies the following computational bounds on $f$. 1. If the strategies are arbitrary quantum channels, then $f\in \mathrm{QSZK}(\mathrm{poly}(T))$, where $\mathrm{QSZK}(T)$ is the class of languages having quantum statistical zero-knowledge proofs in which the verifier runs in time $T$ and the simulator in time $\mathrm{poly}(T)$. 2. If the strategies are Clifford+T circuits using at most $t$ magic gates, then $f\in \mathrm{DTIME}(\mathrm{poly}(T2^t))$. 3. If the strategies are explicit Pauli-sparse unitaries acting on at most $T$ qubits and having at most $s$ nonzero Pauli coefficients, then $f\in \mathrm{DTIME}(\mathrm{poly}(Ts))$. Time and space hierarchies then yield explicit functions secure against superlinear and even all polynomial-time adversaries under our computational restrictions. These bounds exceed the bounded-storage qubit bound $q\leq\log n$ of Bluhm, Christandl, and Speelman (Nature Physics, 2022) for the inner product function $f=\mathrm{IP}$, at the cost of restricting adversarial computation and increasing honest evaluation complexity.
item.dc:creator: Oren Renard, Nicholas Spooner

item.title: Random Quantum Circuits Beyond Moment Matching
item.description: arXiv:2610.02135v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Random quantum circuits aim to efficiently reproduce the statistical properties of ideal random quantum evolution. One approach is to construct approximate unitary designs, which match the moments of Haar-random unitaries up to a prescribed order with controlled error. We establish quantitative guarantees for how accurately these designs reproduce the distribution of each output probability. We show that, for every strong $\varepsilon$-approximate unitary $k$-design on $n$ qubits, the distribution of each output probability is within $O(k^{-1/2}(1+k/2^n)^{-1/2}+\varepsilon)$ in Kolmogorov distance of the Porter-Thomas distribution, a beta distribution with parameters $1$ and $2^n-1$. This bound is optimal up to constant factors, implying that a substantially better uniform bound requires additional structure. We then show that a mild form of local invariance suffices. We prove that any such design that is invariant under unitary translations acting on a single qubit approximates Porter-Thomas to total variation distance $O(k^{-1/2}+\varepsilon)$. Every strong $\varepsilon$-approximate unitary $k$-design invariant on $\log k+O(1)$ qubits achieves error $2^{-\Omega(k)}+O(\varepsilon)$ in Kolmogorov distance and $2^{-\Omega(k)}+O(\varepsilon\log(2/\varepsilon))$ in total variation distance. These results identify the distributional accuracy guaranteed by moment matching and the structure that improves it. As an application, we show that the Shannon entropy of the output distribution of a strong $\varepsilon$-approximate $k$-design is concentrated around its Haar value $n-\Theta(1)$: its mean differs from the Haar mean by $O(k^{-1/4}+\varepsilon^{1/2})$ and its standard deviation is $O(2^{-n/2}+k^{-1/8}+\varepsilon^{1/4})$. Consequently, a trusted device sampling such circuits generates $n-O(1)$ bits of entropy per sample, which makes them useful for random number generation.
item.dc:creator: Shih-Han Hung

item.title: Beyond light cones: State preparation complexity in quantum spin glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.02166v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a technique for studying state preparation complexity in the quantum $p$-spin model on $n$ qubits, a disordered quantum spin system with random interactions on every set of $p$ qubits. We reduce the task of proving state preparation lower bounds to bounding the local profile complexity of the class, a quantity derived from the metric entropy of the set of vectors recording each state's expectation values against all weight-$p$ Pauli strings. We show that, for sufficiently large fixed $p$, any class with local profile complexity $O(n^2)$ remains separated from the ground-state energy by $\Omega(\sqrt n)$, a gap on the leading energy scale. When the profile complexity is $o(n^2)$, we prove the stronger conclusion that the class cannot outperform a benchmark class of simpler states at leading order. Product states always provide such a benchmark. Our framework strengthens known bounds and covers classes beyond the reach of previous methods. These include examples where circuit lightcones extend across the entire system, preventing an application of standard arguments. We obtain an $\Omega(n^2/\log n)$ gate lower bound for preparing near-ground states and depth--width tradeoffs, allowing arbitrary one- and two-qubit gates and arbitrarily many discardable ancillas. We also derive lower bounds on entanglement depth and matrix product state bond dimension, and energy obstructions for forward and reverse magic at every fixed level of Parham's magic hierarchy (arXiv:2504.19966). For Clifford circuits doped with $T$-gates, we obtain sharper energy comparisons using product stabilizer states as a more restrictive benchmark. The proof combines an adaptation of a nonsymmetric quantum de Finetti theorem (arXiv:1810.12197) with metric-entropy bounds for the Gaussian process indexed by the local profiles of states in the class.
item.dc:creator: Omar Al-Ghattas, David Gamarnik, Bobak T Kiani

item.title: Complete Classification of Reversible Entanglement Transformations of Two Qutrits
item.description: arXiv:2610.05234v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study single-copy exact deterministic transformations of bipartite quantum states under local operations and classical communication (LOCC), and give a complete classification of the states in two three-level systems that can be transformed into each other. This classification applies to finite protocols and to the countable protocols specified in this paper.
